title: How weight editing stopped Qwen's thinking loops
excerpt: Astra edited Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights, cutting repetition and raising math accuracy from 7.9% to 48.1% on MATH-500.
body:
Why Qwen got stuck in thinking loops  

Qwen-3.5-0.8B often entered a “thinking mode” where it kept repeating the same reasoning steps until the output token limit was reached. On the MATH-500 benchmark the base model hit that limit on 93 % of attempts, so most answers never produced a final result. The model card for Qwen already warned that sampling settings and streaming detection are needed to break such loops, but the warning does not fix the underlying weight-level cause.  

The loop manifested as a repetition-associated direction inside the feed-forward networks of layers 15 and 19. When the model followed that direction, each new token reinforced the same pattern, exhausting the token budget before a conclusion could be reached. Because the failure was deterministic, every turn on a math problem followed the same path, allowing the authors to target it directly with weight editing.  

## What Astra changed in the weight space  

Astra, the GPT-6 editing model supplied by OpenAI, received access to Qwen’s weights, a tokenizer, and a CPU-only Python kernel. The prompt also provided practice files containing problems, reference solutions, and the model’s own generated texts. Using this environment, Astra inspected activations in layers 15 and 19, identified the repetition-associated direction, and subtracted that contribution from selected output columns. In plain terms, Astra removed the component of the weight matrix that pushed the model toward repeated reasoning.  

The authors describe the operation as “Astra subtracted the repetition-associated direction written by the feed-forward components of layers 15 and 19 from selected output columns, allowing the model to finish more answers.” After the subtraction, Qwen produced complete answers on a larger share of problems, and its reported math accuracy on MATH-500 rose from 7.9 % to 48.1 % under the fixed protocol.  

## How the edit was evaluated  

Evaluation used the same benchmark that reported the accuracy jump: MATH-500, with the protocol disclosed in the prompt. The edited model was tested on questions that were unseen by Astra during the editing process, ensuring that the edit was not over-fitted to the training set.  

Two metrics were reported. First, the percentage of answers that reached the token length cap dropped from 93 % to 33.1 %, indicating that many more completions reached a logical end. Second, the accuracy on the benchmark increased to 48.1 %. The authors note that about a third of edited answers still hit the length cap, so the repair is incomplete but significant.  

The evaluation relied on batched model-run feedback. A generation request could contain up to 512 answers in total; paired comparisons could generate up to 256 answers per model; a teacher-forced request could inspect up to 1 024 texts within token constraints.

Fifty budget units therefore described batches of useful feedback, separate from the count of Python runs, conversation turns, or training steps. No gradient-based training was performed; the edit was a pure weight-space manipulation guided by observed activations and failure counts.

## What Python and practice feedback contributed  

The prompt supplied a persistent CPU Python kernel, a tokenizer, and libraries for numerical analysis. The kernel had no internet or GPU access; model execution happened through a separate forward-pass tool. Practice files contained problems, answers, and, for the GSM8K and MATH training splits, reference solutions.  

Astra could inspect generated texts, grades, failure counts, and internal activations. It could compare original and edited versions on the same problems, providing evidence for choosing a component and testing an intervention. The forward-pass budget required careful reading: a generation request could contain up to 512 answers, paired comparisons up to 256 per model, and teacher-forced requests up to 1 024 texts. These limits defined the “budget units” mentioned in the logs.  

The pinned logs show that the successful Qwen run was a multi-turn process. The editor inspected failures, tried interventions, and compared outcomes across many turns. The narration omits exact wall-clock time because provider wait time inflates the total, but the logs make the iterative nature of the work clear.  

## Limits and follow-up experiments  

The repair remains incomplete. Edited Qwen still hit the length cap in 33.1 % of MATH-500 answers, meaning a sizable queue of requests can still consume the whole budget. The title’s word “patched” reflects that limitation.  

A smaller Gemma model was later used in a follow-up experiment. That study failed to establish a gain, highlighting that the success of weight editing can depend on model size, architecture, and the specific failure being repaired.

Matthew Honnibal’s critique points out that combining experiments with different conditions can create an impression of broader impact than the data support. The source does not claim a universal solution; it frames the Qwen edit as a concrete demonstration of weight-space programming for a known obstacle.

## The takeaway  

Weight editing can directly remove a pathological direction that causes thinking loops, turning many unfinished attempts into complete answers. In the Qwen case, subtracting the repetition-associated component from layers 15 and 19 raised math accuracy dramatically while still leaving room for further improvement.  

When a model repeatedly hits a token limit due to a deterministic activation pattern, locate the responsible weight direction and edit it out. Use a separate editing model with access to the target’s weights, practice data, and feedback loops, then evaluate on unseen benchmark items to confirm that the edit reduces loop frequency and improves task performance.

- [The ‘Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen’ post is misleading](https://honnibal.dev/blog/astra-read-write-misleading)
